title.en: Rat's Wedding and the Burnt Rice

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 56 'Rat's Wedding' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: At his own wedding feast Rat remembers the burnt rice he loves to scrape. Halfway home with his bride he invents a forgotten treasure, leaves her on the water-table, and sneaks to the kitchen — where the burnt-rice pot, disturbed, turns over and traps his head. Craping away in the dark, he is found, lifted, and killed by the cook's helpers: which is why there are so many widows in the world — their husbands died and left them.
summary.zh: 老鼠在自己的婚宴上惦記著愛刮的焦飯。半路撇下新娘，謊稱遺忘貴重之物，溜回廚房——焦飯鍋被碰翻，罩住了他的頭。黑暗中刮飯作響的鼠被廚娘逮個正著，一鍋抬起，當場斃命——世上寡婦之多，正因丈夫死了撇下她們。

sensitivity.note: Folk animal tale with comic ending. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Rat got married, and rice and peas were provided for the dinner. It was so richly cooked and so much that it got burnt. Rat remembered that the rice burnt in the pot, and Rat liked scrapping; while he was going home with his wife in the way, when he got part way he said to her, 'I forget something very valuable in the wedding house — have to go back for it!' She agreed, and he set the buggy out on the water-table and ran back to the wedding house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He never went in where everybody was merrying himself; he went to the kitchen. The pot with the burnt rice was leaning up by the side of the wall. He went to the pot, troubled it, and the pot, instead of rolling away, turned over and covered him underneath. When he found he could not come out he said, 'Chut! What about that? I wouldn't give a biscuit for a man who can't lose his night rest!' — and he began to scrape the burnt part, kur-ur-rup, krup, krup, krup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife was calling now, 'Mr. Rat! Mr. Rat!' — 'Me head fasten in pot-o!' — and he turned back scraping, scraping. The cook heard the noise, went out to the kitchen, found it was Rat underneath the pot, called out for help; they came out, lifted up the pot and killed him. That is why there are so many widows in the world — because their husbands died and left them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57a 'Cock's Breakfast' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Cockroach twice eats Cock's breakfast under the promise of a return meal with an Anansi-style noise-signal that never comes. Creeping back at last with his fiddle — 'Ring a ting ting, me know nigger fe nigger!' — he is heard inside a gourd, cornered, picked up and swallowed; and from that day not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
summary.zh: 蟑螂兩次吃掉公雞的早餐，又以『無聲即開飯』的暗號耍賴不還席。最後他拉琴潛返——『叮叮響，我知黑吃黑！』——卻在葫蘆中被聽破，被公雞堵住、拾起、吞下；自那天起，蟑螂再也不敢踏進雞院半步。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (cockroach/fowl-yard proverb). Beckwith's source text contains period racial idiom in song; paraphrase avoids it.

passages.text: One day Cockroach said to Cock, 'Brar Cock, get a little breakfast, so I will come and have breakfast with you.' Cock said yes. Cockroach came, Cockroach ate; when he had done, he said, 'Brar Cock, when you know my breakfast is ready, come.' — 'How must I know?' — 'I will give you a sign: when you hear me make noise, don't come; but when you hear me stay still in the yard, you must come.' When Cock went, he did not find Cockroach, and returned back to his yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The second day Cockroach came and said, 'O Brar Cock! from the time I left you, pain all over my skin, so I went and lay down; but today you can come.' Cock did the same, went to the yard, did not find him, and returned back. When he got halfway, he heard in Cockroach's house — 'Ring a ting ting!' Cock took time, tiptoed along, and heard Cockroach inside a gourd. Cock took his bill and licked him at the gourd; Cockroach ran out, Cock picked him up and swallowed him. So from that day, not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57c 'The Drum' (told by Mrs. Matilda Hall, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach, hearing music everywhere at Christmas and having none, agree to cut little bits of their own skin to make a drum. Roach claims to have no skin, is driven from the company into a banana tree — and vows to be the first to play the finished drum. On Christmas eve the friends, three-quarters of a mile off at market, hear it sounding under Roach's feet; Puss finds him and kills him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
summary.zh: 聖誕將至，狗、猴、虎、貓與蟑螂聽遍四方音樂而自己一無所有，遂約定各割少許皮來蒙鼓。蟑螂自稱『無皮』，被逐出夥伴、躲進芭蕉樹——卻揚言要第一個敲響此鼓。聖誕前夕，眾友在市集上三哩外便聽見鼓聲——是蟑螂以足擊鼓；貓尋聲而至殺之，貓吃蟑螂之習至今未改。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why cat eats cockroach). Skin-cutting frame is folkloric; no ritual instruction. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once there were Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach. Christmas was coming and they heard music played all about, and they had none. They said, 'We have to make up to make a drum — how will we manage?' And they said, 'The only way is to cut a little of our skin to make a drum.' The Roach said, 'I have none' — so they drove him out of the company and he got into a banana tree to live; then he turned round to them and said, 'I first will play that drum!' — 'How will you get it to play?' they asked him, and he said, 'I first will play it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: They fitted up the drum with the skins and hung it up to get cured. Christmas eve fell; going to the market to buy up all the things, about three quarters of a mile off they heard the drum playing — 'Biddy bwoy! who is playing our drum?' It was Roach, who had taken down the drum, put it between his feet and begun to play, singing his song. The Puss came and saw him and killed him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 58 'Hunter, Guinea-hen and Fish' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: A hunter's clearing is also Guinea-hen's feeding ground, and the two unwitting strangers — one by day, one by night — keep thanking each other for the work. When harvest comes, Guinea-hen calls Fish with a trombone, trades a loan of her wing for his help, and harvests the field with him; at dawn she borrows the wings back 'to catch a butterfly' and sails away, leaving Fish in the furrow. The hunter finds the trembling borrower, is offered a song instead of death, carries the tub of water singing to the sea — and the Fish rides the first big wave home; which is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
summary.zh: 獵人墾的地恰是珠雞的食場——晝人夜禽，互不謀面，卻各自感謝『幫工』。收穫在即，珠雞以號角喚魚，借翼交易同往收穫；天亮前又借『捉蝴蝶』之名收回翅膀遠遁，拋下田中的魚。獵人擒住顫抖的借宿者，魚以歌換命，載歌載舞至海邊，乘巨浪而歸——所以我們總得到海裡才能捕到魚。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why fish live at sea). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Hunter was always hunting, and he met up with a splendid piece of rich land and thought to cultivate it, beginning the same day to cut bush. The piece of land was Guinea-hen's feeding ground; Guinea-hen comes out at night and does not walk in the day. 'Massa is good — he knows this is my feeding ground and begins to clean it, so I can get my pullings clear! Let me help myself,' and she made a little chopping herself too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man came in the morning: 'Hi! thankful! I commenced work yesterday, and massa helped me!' — and did a little more. The third day he burned what he cut — 'Hi! thankful! massa burned the balance!' — and Guinea-hen came at night and gave thanks and cleaned up the balance of what the old man left. Then he planted peas and corn, and Guinea-hen came in the night and said, 'Massa is good! I don't need to plant any' — and began to eat what the old man planted. The old man came in the morning, saw the damage — 'Hi! what insect did this?' — and planted some more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: It went on until the peas began to ripen, about eight weeks. The old man said, 'Going to gather it in tomorrow.' Guinea-hen heard and went to the sea and called the Fish with her trombone: 'I planted a bit of corn and peas, getting ripe, and the old man is coming tomorrow; I want to gather it in tonight before he comes.' Fish accepted — but could neither walk nor fly; Guinea-hen lent her wing and they flew and dropped, and ran, till they came to the ground. 'Here is my own field; gather and eat as much as you like.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When day commenced to light, Guinea-hen saw the old man coming and said it was a butterfly jumping about — 'Lend me your wings, I go catch it for you' — and sailed away quietly out of the field. The old man grumbled, picked what he could, and came to where the Fish was. 'O Fish! is it you who did this damage all this time?' — 'No, not I! Don't kill me and I will sing you some songs.' The old man liked music, put him in a tub of water to sing and dance; Fish said, 'Take me to the nearest sea-side you have.' The old man carried the tub on his head, dancing as the Fish sang, until a big wave came and the Fish aimed for it and went along with it. The old man stayed dancing, not knowing the Fish was gone; he ran home for hook and line and threw it into the sea to catch Fish — and that is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59a 'The Tar Baby' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: The classic sticky capture, Jamaican style: Fox's tar-pole ignores Rabbit's commands until fist, foot and head are fast. Offered the choice of burning, drowning, hanging or dashing over the bramble-patch, the captured rabbit begs for anything but the brambles — and the satisfied Fox hurls him there, to the freedom cheer of 'Oh, what a fool!'
summary.zh: 黏捉經典的牙買加版：福克斯的柏油樁不理兔子的喝令，直到拳、腳、頭逐一粘牢。火燒、溺斃、吊死、拋過荊棘叢——任選其一？被擒的兔子哀求『千萬別拋荊棘』；得意的福克斯便把他拋過荊棘叢——兔子落地歡呼：『哎呀，真是個蠢貨！』

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit tar-baby episode (Jamaican variant); cross-tradition cluster with Anansi tar-baby (Tale 21) and US plantation versions.

passages.text: When Brer Fox tried to catch Brer Rabbit, he could not catch him. He stuck up a tar-pole in his common, and when Brer Rabbit came and saw it, he said, 'Come out of Brer Fox's place, or I kick you!' And the tar-pole wouldn't come out. And he kicked it and his foot fastened. 'Let go foot, else I kick you with the other one!' — and he kicked it with the other one and the other foot fastened. And he boxed it and his hand fastened. 'Let go me, else I box you!' — he boxed it with the other hand and his hand fastened. 'Let it go, else I buck you!' — he bucked it and his head fastened. 'Let me go, else I bite you!' — and when he bit it, his mouth fastened, and he couldn't move or talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Brer Fox said, 'Think I couldn't catch you! Burning you, and drowning you, and hanging you, and dashing you over the bramble — which one would you rather?' He said, 'Do anything you like, but don't dash me over that bramble!' And Brer Fox took him and dashed him over the bramble — and he said, 'Oh, what a fool!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Rabbit's Grace: Bless and Blind Us
title.zh: 兔子哥的禱文：賜福且致盲

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 59b 'Saying Grace' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Captured again, Rabbit asks Fox for a pre-execution prayer — clasp your hands and repeat after me: 'O God, bless and blind us!' Fox, hearing only 'bless and help us', closes his eyes to say it devoutly; the rabbit runs away, and they never see him again.
summary.zh: 兔子再遭擒獲，請求臨刑前做個禱告——『合掌跟著我念：啊上帝，賜福且致盲於我們！』福克斯只聽成『賜福並庇佑』，虔誠閉眼誦念；兔子趁機逃走，從此再無人見過他。

sensitivity.note: Prayer-trick amusement tale; folk-comic use of prayer, not devotional material. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brer Fox caught Brer Rabbit again, and was going to kill him. Brer Rabbit said, 'Do, Brer Fox — as you are going to kill me, have prayers.' And he said, 'Clasp your hands and say what I say: O God, bless and blind us!' But Brer Fox thought he said 'Bless and help us,' and he said it, eyes shut — and Rabbit ran away, and they never saw him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59b (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59c 'Pretending Dead' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Bear comes to Rabbit's yard with news that Fox is dead and needs burying. Rabbit dresses for the funeral — bonpon hat, coatie, spectacles — sits in the rocking-chair and observes that folks who fall down dead always cock a foot in the air and say 'Pooh!' The corpse, taking direction, cocks its foot and says 'Pooh!' — and Rabbit goes away saying a man like that never died yet.
summary.zh: 熊來報喪：福克斯死了，須抬去埋葬。兔子盛裝赴喪——鐵罐高帽、外套、眼鏡——端坐搖椅批評道：『人死倒地，總該翹腳喊一聲噗！』屍體依言翹腳喊了一聲『噗！』——兔子拂袖而去：『你這樣的人，還沒死透呢！』

sensitivity.note: Feigned-death amusement tale (ATU 'pretend dead' cycle). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: When Brer Fox wanted to get Brer Rabbit again, he and Bear made up to catch him. Brer Bear went to Brer Rabbit's yard and told him that Brer Fox was dead and he must help to bury him, for he and Brer Fox were friends. When he got to Brer Fox's yard, he saw Brer Fox lying down. Brer Rabbit put on his bonpon hat and coatie and spectacles, sat up in a rocking-chair and said, 'I never see it so! What a style! What a funniness! I think that when folks fall down dead, they always cock up their foot in the air and make pooh!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Brer Fox cocked up his foot in the air and said, 'Pooh!' — and Brer Rabbit went away and said, 'A man like you never dead yet!' — for a dead man does not take instruction, and the corpse that takes it is only playing. He went home whistling, and the bear and the fox were left to bury nobody, the funeral breaking up over a wooden grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60a 'The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Horse bets Turtle he will reach Kingston first; Turtle stations one of his children at every mile-post with the same travelling-song, the last at the Kingston wharf-house. All night Horse gallops, reining and spurring mile-post to mile-post, each one answering soft and sweet — until at the last post, riding into Kingston, he drops down dead.
summary.zh: 馬與龜賭賽先到京斯頓；龜在每個里程碑各埋伏一個孩子，同唱旅途之歌，最後一個守在碼頭倉房。馬整夜疾馳、勒韁加鞭，每一里程碑都『軟甜』應答——直到最後一站，衝進京斯頓的馬倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Hare/tortoise race cycle (ATU 275) in Jamaican form; family relay trick. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Horse bet Turtle that he would get to Kingston before him. Turtle bet him he would get to Kingston first, Brar Horse. Turtle took up one of his pickney and dropped them at every mile-post, and dropped the last one in at Kingston at the wharf-house, telling them they were going for a sack of salt. The night when they started, as Brar Horse caught up to the first mile-post he sang out in a harsh note — and Turtle answered quite yonder, soft and sweet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Horse said, 'Well! Brar Turtle gone!' Gallop, draw rein, and spur; as he got to the next mile-post he heard the same answer. Gallop and gallop till he got to the next mile-post, and the same song, and at every mile-post the answer soft and sweet from quite yonder — until, as Horse caught to that last mile-post going into Kingston, he dropped down dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60b 'The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Courting the same girl — first into the house in the morning wins — slow-flying Parrot subcontracts a faster cousin: one goes ahead to sit in the tree by her door while the other follows Pigeon behind, answering every taunting call, until the Pigeon, believing Parrot has beaten him in the air, lands beaten outside a house where Parrot is already inside, married to the girl.
summary.zh: 二鳥同追一位姑娘——清早誰先進屋便嫁誰。慢飛的鸚鵡另雇一隻同族：一隻先去她門前樹上候著，一隻跟在鴿子身後應答挑釁之語，直到鴿子以為空中已敗，落在一座鸚鵡早已入內成婚的房子外面，只得留守門外。

sensitivity.note: Race-cycle variant. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Pigeon and Parrot were courting one girl, and she said whichever came first into the house in the morning she would marry. Parrot could not fly very fast; he made a bargain with another Parrot — one went before and left the other to follow Pigeon behind, and the first went near to the girl's house and sat down in a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pigeon called, 'Come on, me pretty Poll!' — and Parrot answered behind, 'Go on, me pretty Pigeon!' Pigeon sailed again and called again; Parrot answered again. When Pigeon nearly caught the house he called again in the same tune — and Parrot answered before him now. Pigeon said, 'Stop! all the while Parrot was behind; how has Parrot got before?' When Pigeon went to the house, Parrot was in the house; Pigeon had to stay outside, and Parrot married the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 62 'Man Is Stronger' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger boasts no one beats their strength; Lion knows there is a little something called 'Man'. The hunter misfires on his first reconnaissance — Tiger flattens a ram-goat, mistaking horns for guns, his belly-scar for a ram-rod, the scrotum for a shot-bag — but the true Man answers Tiger's challenge with a single shot, blood flying all through his body, and Lion gets his 'I told you' over the carcass.
summary.zh: 老虎自誇無人敵得過獅虎之力；獅子深知有個叫『人』的小東西更強。初探時，虎錯把公羊當人——角當槍、腹疤當槍栓、陰囊當彈袋——一掌拍倒。真的人只以一槍應答，血透全身；獅子對著虎屍說：『早跟你說過，如今信了吧！』

sensitivity.note: Animal tale on human supremacy (cf. woodland tradition parallels). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Lion and the Tiger were very good friends. Tiger said, 'No one beats us in strength!' Lion said, 'No, my friend — somebody is stronger than we.' Tiger could not believe it; Lion said there was a little something called Man that was stronger. Tiger said he would have to find that something called Man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went hunting the Man and bucked up Mr. Ram-goat, asked if his name was Man — and whether the two things up here (the horns) were called gun, whether that long scar on his belly was called ram-rod, and whether that bag he had was called shot-bag. Goat said yes. Tiger walked up and licked him flat on the ground, and Goat hollered 'Wi-i! wi-i-i!' Tiger went back to Lion and said he had found something called Man and laid him dead with a single lick. Lion said, 'No, me friend! dat no Man — Man has two feet, and what you tell me has four legs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went out again seeking Man, and a Hunter was out. Tiger saw him — 'Now this yah must be Man!' — and as he went up to the man, the Hunter was aiming for him with the gun. Tiger asked if his name was Man, and the Hunter drove at him with the gun. He ran back to Lion and could only say, 'I find Man, and him single answer — him answer me, blood fly all through me body!' — and he died. Lion said, 'I tell you; you no believe me; but you believe me now!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, ending (1924); not verbatim.
